title: Meaning and Types of Markets
outcomes: Explain what a market means in economics, its elements, and how markets are classified (area, time, transaction, regulation, volume, competition).
Describe the four market structures — perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly — and compare their key features.
Compute total, average and marginal revenue from a schedule and use MR = AR(e − 1)/e.
Apply the two behavioural principles: the shut-down rule (price vs minimum AVC) and profit maximisation at MR = MC.

meta.exam_tip: Expect 2–4 MCQs from this unit: MR from a schedule, MR from elasticity, TR maximum at e = 1, and the shut-down condition. Write MRn = TRn − TRn−1 in rough work every time.

concepts.title: Meaning of market, price and value
body: Goods like air and sunlight are free goods: they are plentiful, so nobody pays for them. Economic goods are scarce compared with what people want; obtaining them means giving up something else (an opportunity cost), so they are traded and carry a price.

Price is the money a buyer must give for one unit of a good or service — the worth of the thing stated in money. Economists separate value in use (how useful a thing is in satisfying a want) from value in exchange (what the thing can fetch in other goods, normally measured in money). Ricardo described exchange value as general command over other purchasable goods. Economics deals with exchange value; purely sentimental value is ignored because the market does not pay for it.

In economics a market is not a building. It is the whole network of buyers and sellers of a product who are in contact — face to face, by phone, through an app or an online portal — and whose dealings settle the price.

Elements of a market: (i) people willing to buy and people willing to sell; (ii) the good or service being traded; (iii) haggling or bargaining that settles the price; (iv) awareness of market conditions among the parties; and (v) one price ruling for that product at any given moment.
concepts.analogy: An online marketplace for used phones has no shop at all, yet it is a full market: thousands of sellers and buyers, one product, haggling in chats, and a going price that everyone soon learns.
concepts.work: When a CA values inventory at net realisable value or tests whether an asset is impaired, the question is "what would this fetch in the market?" — exchange value, not cost and not sentimental value.

concepts.title: Classification of markets
body: Product markets are where households buy goods and services from firms; factor markets are where firms hire land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Product markets allocate goods to consumers; factor markets allocate resources to producers. Prices in factor markets are called factor prices.

By area: local (perishable or bulky goods, local services such as a tailor), regional (a few adjoining states), national (sold throughout one country), international (high-value, low-bulk goods such as gold). With cold chains and air freight, even perishables now reach international markets, so this split is less useful than it once was.

By time (Alfred Marshall): very short period or market period — supply cannot be changed, so price depends only on demand (fresh fish, flowers); short period — output can be changed only by using more or less of the variable factors with the same plant; long period — all factors are variable and the scale of production can change, so supply fully adjusts and the price settled is the normal price; very long or secular period — slow changes in population, capital supply and raw materials.

By nature of transaction: spot (cash) market — goods and money change hands now or within a short time; forward or futures market — delivery and payment on a future date at a price agreed today. By regulation: regulated markets (rules laid down by law, such as a stock exchange) and unregulated or free markets (a weekly village haat). By volume of business: wholesale (bulk, trader to trader — B2B) and retail (small lots to final consumers — B2C). By competition: perfectly competitive and imperfectly competitive.
concepts.analogy: Think of the same mango sold in six ways: in your lane (local), across the country (national), today for cash (spot), booked for next season (forward), in bulk at the mandi (wholesale) and one at a time at the fruit stall (retail).
concepts.work: Hedging advice, contract reviews and audit of derivatives all start with knowing whether a deal is spot or forward; regulated markets also bring disclosure and compliance work for CAs.

concepts.title: Types of market structures
body: A firm can find its most profitable output only if it knows the demand curve for its own product — and that depends on how many rivals it has, how alike their products are and how they react to its price changes. These features together are called market structure.

Perfect competition: very many sellers of an identical product; no single firm can influence the price. Monopolistic competition: many sellers of differentiated (branded) products, e.g. toothpaste or shampoo makers. Oligopoly: a few large sellers whose decisions affect each other, e.g. telecom operators. Monopoly: a single seller of a product with no close substitute, e.g. rail transport by Indian Railways.

Moving from perfect competition to monopoly, the number of sellers falls, product differentiation and control over price rise, and the price elasticity of demand facing the individual firm falls from infinite to small.

concepts.analogy: A vegetable mandi (perfect), a street of cafés each with its own style (monopolistic), three telecom giants watching each other (oligopoly), and the only water supplier in town (monopoly).
concepts.work: Industry analysis in credit appraisal, valuation and equity research begins by placing a company in one of these structures — it tells you how much pricing power and margin to expect.

concepts.title: Total, average and marginal revenue
body: Total revenue (TR) is the money a firm receives from selling a given quantity: TR = P × Q. It equals the total amount buyers spend on the firm's product.
Average revenue (AR) is revenue per unit sold: AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P. Because AR equals price at every quantity, the AR curve is the firm's demand curve.

Marginal revenue (MR) is the change in TR from selling one more unit: MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, or for a one-unit step MRn = TRn − TRn−1 (in calculus terms MR = dTR/dQ, the slope of the TR curve). Adding the MRs of all units sold gives TR: TR = ΣMR.

When the firm must cut the price to sell more, MR is less than the price, because the lower price applies to all the earlier units too. Example: if 4 units sell at ₹50 each and 5 units at ₹47 each, the fifth unit brings ₹47 but the first four now fetch ₹3 less each (₹12), so MR = ₹47 − ₹12 = ₹35 (check: TR 235 − 200 = 35).

With a falling AR, MR falls faster than AR and lies below it; TR rises while MR is positive, is maximum where MR = 0 (slope of TR is zero), and falls when MR turns negative — so the TR curve is shaped like an inverted U. AR can never be zero or negative at a positive output, but MR can be zero or negative.
Under perfect competition the firm sells any amount at the market price, so AR is constant, MR = AR = price, both are one horizontal line, and TR is a straight line rising from the origin.
concepts.analogy: TR is the total in the till; AR is the average bill per item; MR is what the till gained from the very last item rung up.
concepts.work: Pricing proposals that a CA reviews in industry are judged on incremental (marginal) revenue — a discount scheme that lifts volume can still cut total revenue if MR has turned negative.

concepts.title: MR, AR and price elasticity of demand
body: The three are linked by the formula MR = AR × (e − 1) ÷ e, where e is the price elasticity of demand (taken without its minus sign) at that point. Rearranged: e = AR ÷ (AR − MR).
If e > 1 (elastic), MR is positive and TR rises when more is sold at a lower price. If e = 1, MR = 0 and TR is at its maximum. If e < 1 (inelastic), MR is negative and TR falls as more is sold.

On a straight-line demand curve e = 1 at the mid-point, so MR cuts the quantity axis exactly below the mid-point; on the upper half demand is elastic and MR positive, on the lower half demand is inelastic and MR negative.
A profit-maximising firm with a falling demand curve will therefore never choose an output where demand is inelastic, because there MR is negative while MC is always positive.
concepts.analogy: Elastic demand is a crowd that rushes in at a small discount — the till rings louder. Inelastic demand is a crowd that hardly moves — a discount only shrinks the takings.
concepts.work: Before supporting a price cut, a finance controller estimates elasticity from past sales data; if demand is inelastic, the cut will reduce revenue as well as margin.

concepts.title: Behavioural principles of a firm
body: Principle 1 — do not produce at all unless total variable cost is covered. Fixed costs are already committed (sunk) and must be paid whether or not the firm produces, so they do not affect the shut-down decision. If price is below minimum average variable cost (AVC), producing adds to the loss; by shutting down the loss is limited to the fixed cost. Minimum AVC is therefore the shut-down price. Shutting down is a short-run, temporary step, not the same as leaving the industry.

Ranking the cases: price below minimum AVC — shut down; price between minimum AVC and minimum average total cost (ATC) — produce, recover all variable cost and part of fixed cost, but make a loss; price equal to minimum ATC — normal profit (zero economic profit); price above minimum ATC — supernormal (economic) profit.

Principle 2 — expand output up to the point where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. While MR > MC, each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost and raises profit; beyond the point where MR = MC, MC > MR and each extra unit lowers profit. For a true maximum the MC curve must cut the MR curve from below.
concepts.analogy: A taxi driver on a slow night keeps driving if fares at least pay for fuel (variable cost); the car-loan EMI (fixed cost) is due either way. If fares do not even pay for fuel, he parks the car.
concepts.work: CAs in industry apply exactly this logic in "make or shut", special-order and plant-suspension decisions — relevant costs are the avoidable (variable) ones, not the sunk fixed costs.

illustrations.title: Revenue schedule with a falling price
illustrations.q: Vaani Crafts can sell 1 lamp at ₹40, and each extra lamp needs a price cut of ₹4 (price = 44 − 4Q). Prepare a schedule of AR, TR and MR for 1 to 9 lamps. At what output is TR maximum, and what is MR there?

solution.title: Reading the schedule
solution.text: TR rises while MR is positive, reaches its maximum of ₹120 at 5 and 6 lamps (MR of the 6th lamp = 0) and then falls as MR turns negative. AR falls by ₹4 per lamp, but MR falls by ₹8 — twice as fast.
Check: TR at 5 units = sum of the first five MRs = 40 + 32 + 24 + 16 + 8 = ₹120.

illustrations.q: Sarthak Polymers, a price-taking firm, can produce 2,000 units a month. Its average variable cost at that output is ₹34 and monthly fixed cost (rent, permanent staff, interest) is ₹18,000. Should it produce if the market price is (a) ₹40, (b) ₹31?

solution.title: Produce or shut down? (short run)

solution.text: At ₹40 the firm earns a contribution of ₹12,000 towards fixed cost, so producing limits the loss to ₹6,000 against ₹18,000 on shutting down. At ₹31 price is below AVC: producing would lose ₹24,000, more than the fixed cost, so it should shut down for now and restart when price recovers above AVC.

illustrations.title: Profit is highest where MR = MC
illustrations.q: Nidhi Foods faces the price schedule below (₹30 for 1 unit, falling by ₹2 per extra unit). Its total fixed cost is ₹20 and the marginal costs of successive units are ₹22, 16, 12, 18, 26 and 34. Find the profit-maximising output and show that MR = MC there.

solution.text: For units 1 to 3, MR (30, 26, 22) exceeds MC (22, 16, 12), so each adds to profit. For the 4th unit MR = MC = ₹18 — it adds nothing. For the 5th unit MR (₹14) is below MC (₹26), so profit falls from ₹8 to ₹-4.

Profit-maximising output = 4 units (where MR = MC and MC is rising, i.e. MC cuts MR from below); maximum profit = ₹8 (the same profit at 3 units, because the 4th unit adds exactly as much to revenue as to cost).

jobs.title: Will a price cut raise revenue?
jobs.role: CA in industry — commercial finance at a packaged-foods company
jobs.situation: Sales wants to cut the price of a 1 kg pack of atta from ₹62 to ₹58 to "grow revenue". Past promotions show that a similar cut raised volume by about 4%.
steps: Work out the price change: (62 − 58) ÷ 62 ≈ 6.5% fall.
Volume rose about 4% for a 6.5% cut, so elasticity ≈ 4 ÷ 6.5 ≈ 0.6 — demand is inelastic (e < 1).
With e < 1, MR is negative: selling more at the lower price reduces total revenue, before even counting margin.
Recommend non-price tools (bigger pack, visibility, combo offers) or a targeted discount instead of a blanket price cut.
jobs.takeaway: Link MR to elasticity before approving any discount: below e = 1, a price cut lowers revenue.
jobs.think: At what elasticity would the cut leave total revenue roughly unchanged?
jobs.answer: At unit elasticity (e = 1), where MR = 0 and TR is at its maximum.

jobs.title: Suspend the night shift?
jobs.role: CA in practice advising an MSME manufacturer during a slump
jobs.situation: Market prices for the client's castings have fallen. The night shift adds output whose selling price no longer covers power, raw material and shift wages; factory rent and loan interest are paid anyway.
steps: Separate avoidable (variable) costs — power, material, shift wages — from fixed costs that continue anyway.
Compare price with average variable cost of the night-shift output, not with full cost.
If price is below AVC, suspend the shift: the loss falls to the fixed costs that are unavoidable.
Advise that this is temporary — restart when price again exceeds AVC; exit from the industry is a separate long-run question.
jobs.takeaway: The shut-down rule uses variable cost; sunk fixed costs do not decide whether to produce in the short run.

mcqs.q: In economics, the term "market" refers to:
options: Buyers and sellers of a product in contact with one another, whose dealings settle its price
A building where goods are sold
Only the place where wholesale trade happens
The list of goods a shop keeps
mcqs.explain: A market is a network of buyers and sellers, not a place; contact may be online or by phone.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an element of a market?
options: A fixed physical place of trade
mcqs.explain: A market needs buyers and sellers, a product, bargaining, knowledge of conditions and one price at a time — not a fixed place.

mcqs.q: Economics is concerned mainly with:
mcqs.explain: Only exchange value — what a thing fetches in the market — matters in a market economy.

mcqs.q: Markets in which firms buy land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are called:
mcqs.explain: Factor markets allocate productive resources to producers; their prices are factor prices.

mcqs.q: The classification of markets into very short period, short period, long period and secular period is based on:
mcqs.explain: Alfred Marshall introduced the time element in market analysis.

mcqs.q: In the very short period (market period), price is determined mainly by:
mcqs.explain: Supply cannot be changed in the market period, so changes in demand alone move the price.

mcqs.q: The price settled in the long period, when all factors are variable, is called:
mcqs.explain: Long-run supply and demand determine the normal (long-run equilibrium) price.

mcqs.q: A contract to buy US dollars from a bank three months from now at a rate fixed today is a transaction in the:
mcqs.explain: Delivery and payment at a future date at a price agreed now = forward/futures market.

mcqs.q: A stock exchange is an example of a:
mcqs.explain: Transactions on a stock exchange are governed by statutory rules to prevent unfair practices.

mcqs.q: Trade between a manufacturer and a distributor in bulk lots (B2B) takes place in the:
mcqs.explain: Wholesale = bulk, trader-to-trader; retail = small lots to final consumers (B2C).

mcqs.q: Many sellers offering differentiated products to many buyers describes:
mcqs.explain: Differentiation with many sellers is monopolistic competition; perfect competition has identical products.

mcqs.q: The price elasticity of demand facing an individual firm under perfect competition is:
mcqs.explain: The firm's demand curve is horizontal at the market price — perfectly elastic.

mcqs.q: Which market form has a few sellers whose decisions are interdependent?
mcqs.explain: Oligopoly = competition among the few; each firm watches rivals' reactions.

mcqs.q: Average revenue is always equal to:
mcqs.explain: AR = TR ÷ Q = PQ ÷ Q = P. Hence the AR curve is the demand curve.

mcqs.q: A firm sells 10 units at ₹95 each. To sell 11 units it must cut the price to ₹92. MR of the 11th unit is:
A firm earns total revenue of ₹7,200 from selling 90 units. Its average revenue is:
When a firm must lower its price to sell an additional unit, MR is:
mcqs.explain: The lower price applies to earlier units too, so the extra revenue is less than the price.

mcqs.q: Total revenue is maximum when:
mcqs.explain: TR rises while MR > 0 and falls when MR < 0, so it peaks where MR = 0 (e = 1).

mcqs.q: Under perfect competition, the AR and MR curves of a firm are:
options: Downward sloping with MR below AR
mcqs.explain: Price is constant for the firm, so AR = MR = P, a horizontal line.

mcqs.q: Price (AR) is ₹45 and price elasticity of demand is 2.5. Marginal revenue is:
If AR = ₹50 and MR = ₹30, price elasticity of demand is:
mcqs.explain: e = AR ÷ (AR − MR) = 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5. 1.67 is 50/30 (wrong formula).

mcqs.q: When price elasticity of demand is less than one, marginal revenue is:
mcqs.explain: MR = AR(e − 1)/e; with e < 1 the bracket is negative.

mcqs.q: On a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve, MR is zero at:
options: The mid-point of the demand curve
The point where it meets the price axis
The point where it meets the quantity axis
mcqs.explain: Elasticity is one at the mid-point, so MR = 0 there and TR is maximum.

mcqs.q: A firm should shut down in the short run if price is below:
mcqs.explain: Below minimum AVC the firm cannot even cover variable cost; shutting down limits the loss to fixed cost.

mcqs.q: If price lies between minimum AVC and minimum ATC, a firm in the short run will:
mcqs.explain: It covers variable cost and part of fixed cost, so producing gives a smaller loss than shutting down.

mcqs.q: A firm maximises profit at the output where:
options: MR = MC and MC cuts MR from below
mcqs.explain: Profit (not revenue) is maximised where MR = MC with MC rising through MR.

mcqs.q: A price-taking firm has fixed cost ₹50,000, AVC ₹60 and sells 1,000 units at ₹55. Its best short-run choice and resulting loss is:
mcqs.explain: Price ₹55 < AVC ₹60. Producing loses 50,000 + 1,000 × 5 = ₹55,000; shutting down loses only the fixed cost ₹50,000.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: AR can never be negative, but MR can be negative
AR and MR are always equal
TR keeps rising as long as AR is positive
mcqs.explain: Price is never negative, but selling more can reduce TR, making MR negative.

questions.q: Demand for a firm's product is P = 30 − 2Q. (a) Prepare a schedule of AR, TR and MR for Q = 1 to 9. (b) At what output is TR maximum? (c) State the relationship between AR and MR shown by your schedule.

model.text: (b) TR is maximum at ₹112 for 7 and 8 units, where MR becomes zero (MR of the 8th unit = 0). Beyond this MR is negative (-4 for the 9th unit) and TR falls.
(c) AR falls by ₹2 per unit while MR falls by ₹4 per unit: MR is below AR and falls twice as fast; MR = AR only for the first unit; TR = sum of MRs.

scheme.pt: TR computed correctly for all quantities
Identifies TR maximum at 7–8 units where MR = 0
States AR–MR relationship (MR below AR, falls twice as fast)

remarks: Most errors come from computing MR as TR ÷ Q (that is AR).
Candidates who label the columns and show one sample calculation get full credit even with a small slip later.
mistakes: Stopping the schedule at the TR peak and missing negative MR.
Saying TR is maximum where AR is maximum.
tips: Draw a four-column table: Q, AR, TR, MR.
Write MRn = TRn − TRn−1 once at the top.

questions.q: A firm sells its product at ₹120. (a) Find MR when price elasticity is 4 and when it is 0.8. (b) Find elasticity at a point where AR = ₹90 and MR = ₹45. (c) Why would a profit-maximising firm never operate where e = 0.8?

model.text: (b) e = AR ÷ (AR − MR) = 90 ÷ 45 = 2 — demand is elastic, so MR is positive.
(c) With e < 1, MR is negative. MC is always positive, so MR = MC can never hold there; cutting output would raise revenue and lower cost at the same time.

scheme.pt: Reason: MR negative, cannot equal positive MC

remarks: Sign errors on MR at e < 1 are the most common slip.
mistakes: Dropping the minus sign of MR.
tips: Memorise both forms: MR = AR(e − 1)/e and e = AR/(AR − MR).

questions.q: A price-taking firm sells 5,000 units at ₹26 each. AVC is ₹22 and total fixed cost is ₹35,000. Should it continue production in the short run? Show workings. Below what price should it shut down?

model.text: Producing cuts the loss by ₹20,000 (from ₹35,000 to ₹15,000), so the firm should continue. It should shut down if price falls below minimum AVC (here ₹22), when TR would be less than TVC of ₹1,10,000.

scheme.pt: Compares loss on producing with loss on shutting down

remarks: Strong answers state that fixed cost is unavoidable in the short run.
mistakes: Comparing price with ATC and advising closure.
tips: Always show "loss if it produces" next to "loss if it shuts down".

checks.label: TR needed to cover TVC = shut-down point revenue

summary: Market = buyers and sellers in contact who settle a price; it need not be a place.
Elements: buyers and sellers, the good traded, bargaining, knowledge, a single ruling price.
Classified by area, time (Marshall: very short, short, long, secular), transaction (spot/forward), regulation, volume (wholesale/retail) and competition.
Four structures: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
TR = P × Q; AR = TR/Q = P (demand curve); MR = TRn − TRn−1; TR = ΣMR.
MR = AR(e − 1)/e: e > 1 → MR +; e = 1 → MR 0, TR max; e < 1 → MR −.
Shut down if P < minimum AVC; profit maximum where MR = MC and MC cuts MR from below.
remember: Perfect competition: AR = MR = P (horizontal); TR a straight line from the origin.
Falling AR: MR below AR, TR an inverted U.
Minimum AVC = shut-down price; minimum ATC = break-even (normal profit) price.
traps: MR is not TR ÷ Q — that is AR.
TR is maximum where MR = 0, not where profit is maximum.
Shut-down (short run, temporary) is not exit (long run).
Sunk fixed cost does not decide whether to produce in the short run.

quickref.v: ΔTR ÷ ΔQ; MRn = TRn − TRn−1; TR = ΣMR
Produce only if P ≥ minimum AVC
MR = MC, MC cutting MR from below

viva.q: When should a firm shut down in the short run, and why are fixed costs ignored in that decision?
viva.model: A firm should shut down in the short run when price falls below minimum average variable cost, because then it cannot even recover its variable cost. Fixed costs are ignored because they are sunk and have to be paid whether the firm produces or not; by shutting down the loss is limited to the fixed cost. Shutting down is temporary and is not the same as leaving the industry.

viva.q: State the profit-maximising rule for a firm.
viva.model: A firm maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. As long as marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, each extra unit adds to profit, so output should be expanded. The second condition is that the marginal cost curve must cut the marginal revenue curve from below, that is MC must be rising at that point.

viva.q: How did Marshall classify markets on the basis of time?
viva.model: Marshall divided markets by time into four. In the very short or market period supply is fixed, so price depends on demand alone. In the short period supply can be changed only by using more or fewer variable factors with the same plant. In the long period all factors are variable and supply fully adjusts, giving the normal price. The very long or secular period covers slow changes in population, capital and raw materials.

cases.title: Shreya Electricals — pricing a ceiling fan
cases.case: Shreya Electricals sells 1,200 ceiling fans a month at ₹2,000 each. Its marketing head finds that cutting the price to ₹1,900 would raise monthly sales to 1,300 fans. At the present price the finance team estimates the firm's marginal revenue at ₹1,500 a fan. The plant's monthly fixed cost is ₹6,00,000 and its minimum average variable cost is ₹1,200 a fan.

mcqs.q: What is the marginal revenue per fan of the extra 100 fans sold at the lower price?
mcqs.explain: TR rises from ₹24,00,000 to ₹24,70,000, i.e. by ₹70,000 for 100 fans = ₹700 a fan — well below the new price of ₹1,900, because the ₹100 cut applies to all 1,200 earlier fans.

mcqs.q: Using AR = ₹2,000 and MR = ₹1,500, the price elasticity of demand at the present price is:
mcqs.explain: e = AR ÷ (AR − MR) = 2,000 ÷ 500 = 4 — demand is elastic. (1.33 is AR ÷ MR, a common slip.)

mcqs.q: Since MR is positive at the present price, the firm is operating on the:
options: Elastic part of its demand curve
Inelastic part of its demand curve
Horizontal part of its demand curve
mcqs.explain: Positive MR means e > 1.

mcqs.q: If a slump pushed the fan price down to ₹1,100 for a few months, the firm should in the short run:
options: Stop production, because price is below minimum AVC of ₹1,200
Keep producing, because fixed cost must be recovered
Keep producing, because price is above zero
Close the business permanently at once
mcqs.explain: Below minimum AVC the firm cannot cover variable cost; the shutdown is temporary and limits the loss to fixed cost.
